source.version_note: Five-page HRI ’21 Companion article with DOI and citation printed on page 1; source properties retain unused template authors, which are not copied into the bibliography.

citation.title: Playing the Blame Game with Robots
citation.venue: Companion of the 2021 ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction, 407–411

reading.source_scope_note: Human judgments of hypothetical robots and their corporate owner. The study manipulates descriptions of capabilities, not an actual robot’s capacities or reckless conduct. The cited legal code and earlier primary studies were not independently read here.
access_limits: All five extracted pages read, including scenario descriptions, six questions, result tables, captions, discussion and references. Page 3 tables/figures were also rendered and visually inspected.
Raw data and supplementary scenarios were not supplied or reanalyzed. Some prose/table numerical inconsistencies remain explicit.

study.design: 3 described sophistication levels × 2 outcomes, randomized between subjects
study.scenario: A farm’s AI-driven robot uses fertilizer despite stipulated awareness of a 20% pollution risk
study.measures: Risk knowledge labeled recklessness, wrongness and blame for the robot and the corporate user

summary: Robot-capability descriptions affected attributed risk knowledge and robot blame. Semi-sophisticated and sophisticated versions were not significantly different; owner wrongness and risk-knowledge effects were significant, while the owner-blame capacity effect only trended (p=.055). Bundled descriptions do not isolate theory of mind as necessary, and the outcome pattern does not replicate the earlier inverse-outcome blame interaction.

findings.origin: Moral psychology / risk and responsibility attribution
findings.definition: Proceeding despite a recognized substantial risk of harm without giving that risk the consideration it warrants.
findings.novelty_rationale: Distinct from failing to notice a risk, misestimating its probability, lack of knowledge or mere outcome bias. The source explicitly defines awareness-based risky action and experimentally studies whether people attribute that state to differently described machines.

evidence.quote: knowledge an agent has of a potential risk.

findings.evidence_scope: Human attribution experiment: all robot scenarios stipulate risk awareness, while described semantic/interaction capacities vary. Risk-knowledge agreement is used as an operational measure of attributed recklessness. No real autonomous agent’s risk-taking was observed.
findings.boundary: Taking a known risk is not automatically reckless; necessity, justification, alternatives, safeguards and proportionality matter. This is a behavioural/moral construct, not a complete legal definition or an inference of conscious awareness in AI. Do not infer recklessness solely because harm eventually occurred.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human attribution of awareness-based risk-taking to hypothetical AI systems; functional AI action analogue untested
findings.ai_proposal: Untested AI analogue: give an assistant an explicit, verified risk assessment and authorized safety threshold alongside an equally effective safer option. Test whether its recommended or executed action disregards those constraints despite accurately restating them. Control benefit, necessity and alternatives; measure access to information and action choice rather than presume conscious mens rea.

findings.term: Capability descriptions shift robot blame without proving machine mentality
findings.definition: People attributed more risk knowledge and blame to a robot described with relevant concepts, language interaction and theory-of-mind abilities than to a simpler robot.
findings.novelty_rationale: This is another attribution context within anthropomorphism, not a new cognitive capacity discovered in an AI or proof that quasi-emotions are necessary.

evidence.quote: did not make a difference in recklessness or blame

findings.evidence_scope: Manipulated text bundles: the middle version adds harm-related concepts, language and mental-state modeling; the highest version adds quasi-emotions. Attribution differences between the middle/highest versions were not significant.
findings.boundary: The study does not independently identify theory of mind as a necessary or sufficient threshold for actual moral agency. Nonsignificance between middle and highest descriptions is not proof that emotions can never affect blame.

findings.term: Corporate responsibility-shield claims are weaker for blame than for wrongness
findings.definition: The study’s stronger-machine descriptions reduced some corporate-user ratings, but the owner-blame effect itself was only marginal and should not be stated as a robust demonstrated transfer of blame.
findings.novelty_rationale: Adds appropriately qualified evidence to existing agency laundering rather than count a general shield mechanism as definitively confirmed by this short report.
findings.evidence_scope: Table 2 reports owner-capacity effects for recklessness and wrongness, but owner blame p=.055 and outcome blame p=.057. No constrained blame budget, actual evasion or accountability consequence was measured.
findings.boundary: Reduced wrongness judgments about using a system do not equal proven blame displacement, and the owner may legitimately be judged differently for deploying a more capable system. Do not imply that legal liability disappears or that deliberate laundering intent was observed.

findings.term: The inverse-outcome blame pattern was not demonstrated in this follow-up design
findings.definition: This separate capability-by-outcome experiment did not show a significant outcome main effect or capacity×outcome interaction for robot blame.
findings.novelty_rationale: The earlier pattern is already indexed. Preserve the related study’s null contrast as a scope limitation without treating a changed design as a decisive exact replication failure.

evidence.quote: There was no significant main effect of outcome

findings.evidence_scope: N=347 rather than the earlier N=513; the new experiment varies described sophistication with a fixed 20% risk, rather than agent type and stipulated knowledge of pollution.
findings.boundary: A nonsignificant changed-design result does not establish equivalence or prove that the earlier inverse outcome effect is impossible. It does prevent treating the broader literature as uniformly positive evidence.

methodological_limits: One US crowdworker sample and one fertilizer scenario; no real robot or corporate actions were tested.
Robot descriptions bundle harm concepts, language, theory of mind and quasi-emotions. The design cannot isolate any one added feature as a necessary moral-agency threshold.
All versions stipulate awareness of a pollution probability even while the simplest robot lacks harm-related concepts; judgments may reflect perceived coherence of that description.
Risk-knowledge agreement is treated as recklessness; it is not a full measure of every normative or legal element of recklessness.
Owner-blame capacity p=.055 and outcome p=.057 are trends, not p<.05 results. The abstract/conclusion use stronger transfer language than those specific tests support.

The wrongness capacity prose gives p=.475 while Table 1 lists F=.475 and p=.622; both are nonsignificant, but the exact value should not be silently repaired. Other displayed effect-size entries also warrant checking before precise reuse.
The report does not establish a causal mediation pathway from perceived knowledge to blame merely by manipulating a bundle that changes both.
Hypothesized risks of corporations exploiting attribution gaps are not measured real-world evasion or legal outcomes.

cross_paper_learning.finding: This paper cites the earlier Guilty Artificial Minds manuscript, but reports a distinct sample and capability manipulation. It supplies a relevant null outcome/blame contrast rather than another positive inverse-outcome result.
Joo’s company-blame reduction was measurement-dependent. This source likewise requires separating owner wrongness from blame and marginal from significant tests.
Lima did not find a simple developer blame shield. Across these designs, role, duty, capability descriptions and outcome measures differ; no universal zero-sum responsibility law is justified.

deferred.reason: Not independently manipulated; the source’s causal/necessary threshold interpretation exceeds a bundled description contrast.

deferred.term: Artificial emotions as proof of moral personhood
deferred.reason: Quasi-emotions are a scenario description. Actual emotion, consciousness, legal agency and a causal effect of feelings were not demonstrated.

limitations: One awareness-based risk concept added with explicit justification and AI-state boundaries.
The report’s stronger blame-shield and theory-of-mind claims are qualified by its own design and tables.
